questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. How does the Harsanyi transformation turn this into a single extensive-form game?
options: Each player draws her own type from her own prior, then the original game is played.
Nature draws $\theta$ from $p$ and reveals it to all players, then the original game is played.
Nature draws $\theta$ from $p$, each player observes only $\theta_i$, then the original game is played.
The players first announce their types, then play the game for the announced profile.

questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. The Harsanyi transformation draws this game as an extensive-form tree in which Nature moves first. What kind of game is the resulting tree?
options: A game of complete but imperfect information.
A game of complete and perfect information.
A game of incomplete but perfect information.
A game of incomplete and imperfect information.

questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. The Harsanyi transformation draws this game as an extensive-form tree in which Nature moves first. Which decision nodes of player 1 belong to the same information set after Nature's move?
options: Nodes that differ only in player 1's own type $\theta_1$.
Nodes that differ only in player 2's type $\theta_2$.
Nodes that Nature reaches with the same prior probability.
All of player 1's nodes, since Nature's move is hidden from her.

questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. In its Harsanyi tree, with Nature moving first, what is a pure strategy of player $i$?
options: One action $a_i\in A_i$, chosen before Nature moves and used whatever her type.
An action for each of Nature's branches, which amounts to a map $s_i\colon\Theta\to A_i$.
An action at each of her information sets, which amounts to a map $s_i\colon\Theta_i\to A_i$.
A probability distribution over Nature's moves that represents her belief about $\theta$.

questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_1\in\{a,b\}$ and $\theta_2\in\{x,y\}$ and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. The common prior $p$ makes the types correlated, so $p(\theta_1,\theta_2)\neq p(\theta_1)p(\theta_2)$ for some profile. How does the Harsanyi transformation handle this correlation?
options: Nature draws the whole profile $\theta$ with probabilities $p(\theta)$; the rest of the construction is unchanged.
Nature draws $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ independently from the marginals of $p$, since a chance move has no memory.
It cannot be applied, because the transformation needs the types to be independent across the players.
Player $i$'s information sets are indexed by the whole profile $\theta$, since her type is informative about $\theta_{-i}$.

questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. Types are low or high, independently, with $P(\theta_1\text{ low})=0.3$ and $P(\theta_2\text{ low})=0.6$. In the Harsanyi tree, what probability does Nature give the branch ($\theta_1$ high, $\theta_2$ low)?

Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. Here $\Theta_1=\{a,b,c\}$ and $\Theta_2=\{x,y\}$. In the Harsanyi tree, player 1 moves right after Nature's move. How are player 1's decision nodes partitioned into information sets?
options: 2 information sets of 3 nodes each
3 information sets of 2 nodes each
6 information sets of 1 node each
1 information set of 6 nodes

questions.question: Two players choose $C$ (contribute) or $D$ (decline); a good worth $1$ to each is provided if at least one contributes, and contributing costs the contributor her private type $\theta_i$. Costs are $\theta_i\in\{\tfrac{1}{4},2\}$. In the Harsanyi tree, Nature draws $(\theta_1,\theta_2)=(2,\tfrac{1}{4})$ and the players choose $(D,C)$. Which payoff pair $(v_1,v_2)$ is at this terminal node?

Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. Player 1 has two types and three actions. In the Harsanyi tree, how many pure strategies does she have?

Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. Here $|\Theta_1|=3$, $|\Theta_2|=2$, player 1 has $2$ actions and player 2 has $3$. In the Harsanyi tree with player 1 drawn moving before player 2, how many terminal nodes are there?

Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. Each player has at least two types. In the Harsanyi tree, why does subgame perfection add nothing beyond Nash equilibrium of this tree?
options: Every node after Nature starts a subgame, and Nash equilibrium is already optimal in each.
The only subgame is the whole game, so the two concepts coincide.
Nature's move is a subgame of its own, and Nature is not a player whose choices need checking.
Subgame perfection never refines Nash equilibrium in trees that contain a chance move.

questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. When this game is redrawn as a Harsanyi tree, what changes compared with the original game?
options: The payoffs, which are replaced by expected payoffs averaged over Nature's move.
The type spaces, which are merged into a single commonly observed profile.
Only the order of moves and the information sets; payoffs stay $v_i(a;\theta)$.
The action sets, which become one action per type profile for each player.

questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. Before Harsanyi, analysing such a game seemed to need beliefs about payoffs, beliefs about those beliefs, and so on. How does the transformation deal with this?
options: It cuts the regress after two levels, which suffices for players who are rational.
It lets each player choose a belief about the others' payoffs freely at each level.
It makes every player's payoff function known, so beliefs about payoffs are unnecessary.
It replaces the regress by one chance move whose probabilities everyone knows.

questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. Types are $\theta_1\in\{a,b\}$, $\theta_2\in\{x,y\}$ with $p(a,x)=0.3$, $p(a,y)=0.1$, $p(b,x)=0.2$, $p(b,y)=0.4$. At player 1's information set for type $a$, what probability does she assign to the node with $\theta_2=x$?

Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. Player 1 has a single type and three actions; player 2 has two types. In the Harsanyi tree, player 1 moves right after Nature. Which pair (information sets of player 1, pure strategies of player 1) is correct?

Two players choose $C$ (contribute) or $D$ (decline); a good worth $1$ to each is provided if at least one contributes, and contributing costs the contributor her private type $\theta_i$. Costs are $\tfrac{1}{4}$ (low) with probability $0.6$ or $2$ (high), independently. Both players use: contribute if low, decline if high. In the Harsanyi tree, what is player 1's expected payoff before Nature moves?

Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\{\text{low},\text{high}\}$ and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. The players disagree about the prior: player 1 believes $\theta_2$ is low with probability $0.8$, while player 2, before learning $\theta_2$, believes this probability is $0.5$. Why can the Harsanyi transformation not be applied as stated?
options: There are no Nature probabilities that all players share, so no single commonly known tree.
Because the two probabilities differ, while Nature must give every type equal probability.
Because the transformation needs each player to know the other player's realized type.
Because the payoffs $v_i(a;\theta)$ would differ between the two players' versions of the tree.

questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_i\in\Theta_i$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and act simultaneously; payoffs are $v_i(a;\theta)$. In the Harsanyi tree, type $\theta_1=b$ has prior probability $0$ while all other types have positive probability. What does a Nash equilibrium of the tree require of player 1's action at type $b$'s information set?
options: Nothing: changing it does not change player 1's expected payoff.
It must be a best response for type $b$, as at every information set of the tree.
It must match type $a$'s action, since a zero-probability type copies a reachable type.
It must be removed from the tree, since Nature never draws a zero-probability type.

questions.question: Players 1 and 2 privately know their types $\theta_1\in\{a,b,c\}$ and $\theta_2\in\{x,y\}$, drawn from a common prior $p$, and choose $C$ or $D$ simultaneously. In the Harsanyi tree, Nature moves first, then player 1, then player 2. How are player 2's decision nodes partitioned into information sets?
options: 4 information sets of 3 nodes each
3 information sets of 4 nodes each
2 information sets of 6 nodes each
12 information sets of 1 node each

questions.question: Player 1 has types $\{a,b\}$ and chooses one of three actions after Nature's move; player 2 has types $\{x,y,z\}$ and moves next, observing player 1's action but not $\theta_1$. In the Harsanyi tree, how are player 2's decision nodes partitioned into information sets?
options: 3 information sets of 6 nodes each
9 information sets of 2 nodes each
18 information sets of 1 node each
6 information sets of 3 nodes each
